title: Computer Science and Computer Engineering for Games

volumes.title: Mathematics for Games and Computing
volumes.purpose: Build the mathematical language for algorithms, graphics, physics, signals and experiments.

modules.title: Discrete mathematical reasoning
modules.prerequisites: Volume 01; complete the algebra diagnostic in START_HERE before proceeding.
modules.project: Write a mathematical notebook containing a truth-table specification, an induction proof, a graph model and a justified operation-count estimate. Include counterexamples to three false claims.

lessons.title: Algebra, functions, logarithms and trigonometry
lessons.outcome: Translate a game relationship into an equation with a defined domain.
lessons.teach:
A function maps each allowed input to one output. Its domain matters: dividing by zero or taking a real square root of a negative number is not repaired by notation. Rearranging an equation must preserve its conditions. Exponents model repeated multiplication; logarithms invert exponentiation. log2(n) often counts how many times a size can be halved.
Angles connect geometry to periodic motion. In radians, a full revolution is 2*pi. For a unit circle, a direction at angle t has components (cos(t), sin(t)). Check units before calling a trigonometric function. Degrees and radians are different representations of the same angle, not interchangeable numeric inputs.
lessons.example: At 90 degrees, or pi/2 radians, the unit-circle direction is (0, 1). A list of 1024 items can be halved ten times to reach one because 2^10 = 1024.
lessons.lab: Solve distance = speed*time for each variable and state forbidden inputs. Convert 0, 90, 180 and 360 degrees to radians. Pass: solve ten algebra problems and explain logarithms using repeated halving before advancing.
lessons.reading: R08: prerequisite algebra review and trigonometric functions; R06: sums and asymptotics.

quiz.question: What is log2(64)?
quiz.answer: 6, because 2^6 = 64.

quiz.question: Convert 180 degrees to radians.
quiz.answer: pi radians.

quiz.question: What restriction applies when computing speed = distance/time?
quiz.answer: Time cannot be zero; also state the physical units and whether negative time is meaningful.

lessons.title: Logic, sets and quantified claims
lessons.outcome: Express requirements precisely enough to test or prove.
lessons.teach:
Propositional logic combines true/false statements. Implication P -> Q fails only when P is true and Q is false. It does not claim that P actually happens. A universal claim says a property holds for every allowed input; an existential claim says at least one input has it. Negating a universal claim requires one counterexample.
Sets group distinct elements; relations describe connections; functions are relations with exactly one output for each domain element. These ideas support requirements such as every live entity has one valid transform. Ambiguous language like "usually valid" cannot serve as an invariant until its exceptions are specified.
lessons.example: "Every saved entity has an ID" is disproved by one saved entity without an ID. "Some entity is visible" requires only one witness and does not imply all entities are visible.
lessons.lab: Formalize five requirements for the grid game using sets and quantifiers. Construct truth tables for a door-access rule. Pass: provide a counterexample or witness for each negated requirement.
lessons.reading: R06: propositions, predicates, sets and relations.

quiz.question: When is P -> Q false?
quiz.answer: When P is true and Q is false.

quiz.question: Negate "every unit has positive health."
quiz.answer: There exists a unit whose health is not positive.

quiz.question: Why must the domain of a quantified statement be explicit?
quiz.answer: The claim can change meaning or truth when it ranges over different objects or inputs.

lessons.title: Proofs, induction and invariants
lessons.outcome: Justify a program property instead of testing only examples.
lessons.teach:
A proof is a chain of justified steps from assumptions to a conclusion. Direct proof, contradiction and induction solve different kinds of questions. Induction establishes a base case and shows that validity at one step implies validity at the next. Both parts are necessary.
A loop invariant connects mathematical reasoning to implementation: establish it before the loop, preserve it in each iteration, and combine it with the exit condition to prove the result. Testing complements proofs by checking whether code matches the modeled assumptions. A proof of an ideal algorithm does not automatically establish the correctness of its floating-point implementation.
lessons.example: To prove the running sum after k iterations equals 1+...+k, start at k=0 with sum=0. If the claim holds at k, adding k+1 produces the required sum for k+1.
lessons.lab: Prove the formula 1+...+n = n(n+1)/2 by induction. Then write an invariant for counting living units in a prefix of a list. Pass: show initialization, preservation and termination explicitly.
lessons.reading: R06: induction, invariants and proof methods.

quiz.question: What are the two essential parts of induction?
quiz.answer: A valid base case and an implication from the inductive hypothesis to the next case.

quiz.question: Why does a mathematical proof not eliminate implementation tests?
quiz.answer: The code, machine arithmetic or environmental assumptions may differ from the proven model.

lessons.title: Counting, graphs and recurrences
lessons.outcome: Model combinations and recursive work without brute-force guessing.
lessons.teach:
The product rule counts independent sequential choices; the sum rule counts disjoint alternatives. A graph represents vertices and edges, which may be directed or weighted. A level map, dependency graph and network topology are different applications of the same abstraction. Decide what an edge means before choosing an algorithm.
A recurrence describes a quantity in terms of smaller instances. Repeatedly halving a search space gives logarithmic depth, but doing linear work at every level changes total cost. Do not confuse possible states with states actually explored by a particular algorithm. Counting provides upper bounds and exposes when exhaustive search becomes unrealistic.
lessons.example: Four independent equipment slots with three choices each give 3^4 = 81 combinations. An undirected simple graph with n vertices has at most n(n-1)/2 edges because each unordered pair appears once.
lessons.lab: Build a dependency graph for game startup and identify an invalid cycle. Count loadout combinations with and without a restriction. Pass: explain the recurrence for halving a search range and distinguish depth from total work.
lessons.reading: R06: counting, graphs, recurrences and asymptotic notation.

quiz.question: How many combinations arise from five independent binary choices?
How many edges can a simple undirected graph with five vertices have?
Why is a dependency cycle a problem for a simple startup order?
quiz.answer: No member can be initialized first while requiring another member of the cycle to be ready.

modules.title: Linear algebra and game geometry
modules.project: Build a tested vector/matrix library for a two-dimensional scene, then demonstrate a three-dimensional camera transformation with written coordinate conventions.

lessons.title: Vectors, dot products and projections
lessons.outcome: Use vectors for direction, distance and component measurements.
lessons.teach:
A vector represents a magnitude and direction in a chosen coordinate system. A point represents a location; subtracting points yields a displacement vector. The Euclidean length of (x,y,z) is sqrt(x*x+y*y+z*z). Normalization divides by length, so the zero vector needs a deliberate policy.
The dot product measures alignment and produces a scalar. For unit vectors it equals the cosine of the included angle. Projection onto a unit direction u is dot(v,u)*u. In three dimensions the cross product produces a perpendicular vector with orientation determined by the coordinate convention. Do not use a cross-product sign without declaring handedness.
lessons.example: For v=(3,4), length is 5 and its unit direction is (0.6,0.8). Dotting v with u=(1,0) gives 3, the component along the x axis.
lessons.lab: Implement length, dot and safe normalization. Use dot products to determine whether a target is in front of a character. Pass: test zero vectors, perpendicular vectors and opposite directions.
lessons.reading: R07: vectors and projections; R23: Geometry and Transformations / Vectors.

quiz.question: What is the length of (6,8)?
What is the dot product of (1,0) and (0,1)?
quiz.answer: 0, indicating perpendicular directions.

quiz.question: Why cannot the zero vector be normalized by the ordinary formula?
quiz.answer: Its length is zero, so division is undefined and it has no unique direction.

lessons.title: Matrices, bases and linear systems
lessons.outcome: Understand a matrix as a transformation rather than a table to memorize.
lessons.teach:
A matrix describes how basis vectors are mapped. Matrix-vector multiplication combines those images to transform a vector. A basis is a set of independent directions spanning the space. Changing basis changes coordinates without necessarily changing the underlying geometric object.
Matrix multiplication composes transformations, and order generally matters. Solving Ax=b is not the same task as explicitly computing A inverse; elimination or factorization is often preferable. A singular matrix loses information and cannot be uniquely inverted. In graphics, a zero scale along an axis is a concrete example of collapsing multiple points to the same location.
lessons.example: In two dimensions, scaling x by 2 maps (1,1) to (2,1). Rotating and then applying a nonuniform scale generally differs from applying the scale and then rotating.
lessons.lab: Implement 2-by-2 multiplication and solve two small linear systems by elimination on paper. Pass: show a pair of transforms that do not commute and explain a singular example geometrically.
lessons.reading: R07: matrix multiplication, elimination, inverses and vector spaces.

quiz.question: Do matrices generally satisfy AB = BA?
quiz.answer: No. Transformation order usually changes the result.

quiz.question: What happens to invertibility when an axis is scaled to zero?
quiz.answer: Information on that axis is lost, making the transformation singular.

quiz.question: Why solve Ax=b without explicitly forming an inverse?
quiz.answer: Factorization can be more efficient and numerically preferable, especially for repeated or large solves.

lessons.title: Homogeneous transforms, cameras and quaternions
lessons.outcome: Compose a scene using explicit coordinate conventions.
lessons.teach:
Homogeneous coordinates allow translation to be represented with matrix multiplication. In a common three-dimensional convention, points use w=1 and directions use w=0. A model transform maps local coordinates into world space; a view transform maps world coordinates into camera space. Perspective projection introduces a division by w and changes how depth is represented.
Choose row or column vectors, multiplication order, handedness and depth range, then document them. A unit quaternion represents orientation compactly and supports interpolation, but multiplication order still matters and accumulated error may require normalization. Euler angles remain useful for interfaces; their limitations do not make them meaningless.
lessons.example: With column vectors and a local-to-world matrix M, a point is p_world=M*p_local. A parent-child chain is M_parent*M_child*p_local. Reversing it changes the coordinate interpretation.
lessons.lab: Create a parented object and camera using documented conventions. Pass: test identity, inverse round trips within tolerance, a translated direction that remains unchanged, and a parent rotation that moves its child correctly.
lessons.reading: R23: Coordinate Systems and Transformations; R19: geometric transformations.

quiz.question: Why commonly use w=0 for directions?
quiz.answer: Translation should not change a pure direction; the homogeneous form makes the translation term vanish.

quiz.question: What does the view transform do?
quiz.answer: It expresses world-space geometry in the camera coordinate system.

quiz.question: Why document multiplication order even when using a library?
quiz.answer: The library convention and application convention must agree; otherwise valid arithmetic produces the wrong geometry.

lessons.title: Eigenvalues, least squares and singular values
lessons.outcome: Recognize stability and approximation problems in game data.
lessons.teach:
An eigenvector keeps its direction under a linear transformation; its eigenvalue is the scale applied along that direction. These concepts help analyze repeated updates and dynamical systems. Least squares fits an approximate solution when equations are inconsistent or measurements are noisy. It minimizes a chosen squared residual, not necessarily every meaningful error.
Singular values describe how strongly a matrix stretches different directions. Very small singular values can make inversion sensitive to input errors. Condition number measures sensitivity of the problem; algorithmic stability concerns how a method handles arithmetic error. A well-written algorithm cannot remove information absent from a badly conditioned problem.
lessons.example: The diagonal matrix diag(2,0.5) stretches the x direction by 2 and y by 0.5. Repeated application expands one component while shrinking the other.
lessons.lab: Fit a line to five noisy position/time observations and report residuals. Analyze repeated multiplication by a diagonal matrix. Pass: distinguish data noise, poor conditioning and a programming error in your report.
lessons.reading: R07: eigenvalues, least squares and singular value decomposition.

quiz.question: What are the eigenvalues of diag(3,2)?
quiz.answer: 3 and 2, with the coordinate axes as eigenvector directions.

quiz.question: What objective does ordinary least squares minimize?
quiz.answer: The sum of squared residuals under its specified model.

quiz.question: Can a stable algorithm make an ill-conditioned problem insensitive?
quiz.answer: No. It can limit added numerical error but cannot eliminate the problem's inherent sensitivity.

modules.title: Calculus, mechanics and numerical simulation
modules.prerequisites: Modules 06.1 and 07.1; work through the linked calculus problem sets.
modules.project: Build a projectile and spring simulator with analytic comparison cases, timestep refinement, unit checks and a report separating model error from numerical error.

lessons.title: Limits, derivatives and rates
lessons.outcome: Connect derivatives to velocity, acceleration and local approximation.
lessons.teach:
A derivative measures the local rate of change of a function. Velocity is the derivative of position with respect to time; acceleration is the derivative of velocity. The derivative carries units: meters differentiated by seconds gives meters per second. Product and chain rules explain how composed calculations change.
A finite difference approximates a derivative from samples. Making the step smaller reduces some approximation errors but can worsen floating-point cancellation. The derivative of an ideal formula and the difference between two measured samples answer related but not identical questions. Always distinguish the mathematical function from the noisy or discretized data available to your program.
lessons.example: For x(t)=t*t, velocity is 2*t. At t=3, velocity is 6. The forward difference using h=0.1 is ((3.1)^2-3^2)/0.1=6.1, an approximation rather than the exact derivative.
lessons.lab: Compare analytic and finite-difference derivatives of three functions over several step sizes. Pass: include units, an error table and an explanation of why the smallest tested h need not be best.
lessons.reading: R08: differentiation, product rule and chain rule.

quiz.question: Differentiate x(t)=3*t*t.
quiz.answer: dx/dt = 6*t.

quiz.question: What units does acceleration have when position is in meters?
quiz.answer: Meters per second squared.

quiz.question: Why can excessively small finite-difference steps be inaccurate?
quiz.answer: Subtracting nearly equal floating-point values magnifies rounding and cancellation error.

lessons.title: Integrals, accumulation and continuous probability
lessons.outcome: Interpret integration as accumulated contribution.
lessons.teach:
An integral accumulates contributions over a domain. Integrating velocity over time gives displacement; integrating acceleration changes velocity. The fundamental theorem of calculus connects derivatives and integrals. A definite integral is a signed accumulation, so negative contributions can cancel positive ones.
Numerical quadrature approximates an integral with samples and weights. Rectangle, trapezoid and higher-order rules have different accuracy assumptions. More samples do not repair a wrong model or omitted discontinuity. In graphics, integration will later accumulate incoming light over directions; in probability, a density integrates to a probability over an interval.
lessons.example: With constant velocity 4 meters/second over 3 seconds, displacement is 12 meters. For v(t)=2*t from 0 to 3, integrating gives 9 meters, not the final velocity multiplied by the whole duration.
lessons.lab: Implement rectangle and trapezoid integration for v(t)=2*t and a curved function. Pass: compare to an analytic integral, halve the step and report how error changes.
lessons.reading: R08: integration and the fundamental theorem; R23: Monte Carlo Integration introduction.

quiz.question: Integrate constant velocity 5 over two seconds.
quiz.answer: Displacement is 10 units of length.

quiz.question: What is the integral of 2*t from 0 to 3?
quiz.answer: [t^2] from 0 to 3 = 9.

quiz.question: Why can an integral be zero despite nonzero motion?
quiz.answer: Positive and negative displacement can cancel; total distance is a different quantity.

lessons.title: Newtonian mechanics and differential equations
lessons.outcome: Model motion from forces with clear simplifying assumptions.
lessons.teach:
Newton's second law relates net force to mass times acceleration. Position and velocity form the state of a basic particle model. Gravity, springs and damping provide forces with different dependencies. A differential equation specifies how state changes; initial conditions select a particular trajectory.
For a simple spring, force is proportional to displacement from rest and opposite its sign. Damping depends on velocity and dissipates energy in the model. Distinguish mass from weight and force from impulse. Games often choose simplified models for control and performance; simplification is legitimate when its behavior and limitations are explicit.
lessons.example: A 2 kg body under a constant 6 N net force has acceleration 3 m/s^2. Over 0.5 seconds, its velocity changes by 1.5 m/s. This says nothing about drag unless drag is included in the net force.
lessons.lab: Implement a particle under constant acceleration and a damped spring. Pass: compare the constant-acceleration trajectory to its analytic solution and state what collision, rotation and air-resistance effects are omitted.
lessons.reading: R28: simulation, bodies, forces and impulses; R08: differential-equation applications.

quiz.question: What acceleration results from 10 N on a 2 kg mass?
How does impulse differ from force?
quiz.answer: Impulse is force integrated over time and changes momentum; force is a rate of momentum change.

quiz.question: Why must initial conditions accompany a differential equation?
quiz.answer: Many trajectories can satisfy the same differential rule; initial state selects the intended one.

lessons.title: Time integration, stability and error
lessons.outcome: Choose and test a numerical update rather than assuming smaller code is correct.
lessons.teach:
Explicit Euler advances state using derivatives at the old state. Semi-implicit Euler updates velocity first and then uses the new velocity for position. Other methods trade more work for different accuracy and stability properties. A method can have small local error yet accumulate unacceptable global drift.
Timestep choice depends on the system, method and acceptable error. Stiff springs can require much smaller explicit steps than slow motion. Fixed timesteps aid repeatability but do not guarantee stability or identical results across machines. Compare against analytic cases, inspect energy where meaningful and repeat with a refined step before trusting a visually plausible animation.
lessons.example: For explicit Euler: x_next=x+v*dt; v_next=v+a*dt. For semi-implicit Euler, compute v_next first and use x_next=x+v_next*dt. The methods differ even with identical inputs.
lessons.lab: Compare explicit and semi-implicit Euler on an undamped spring at three timesteps. Pass: plot or tabulate position and energy error, identify an unstable case, and avoid calling visual smoothness proof of physical accuracy.
lessons.reading: R23: physically based animation topics via R19; R28: simulation stepping guidance.

quiz.question: Which velocity does semi-implicit Euler use for the position update?
quiz.answer: The newly updated velocity.

quiz.question: Does a fixed timestep guarantee a stable simulation?
quiz.answer: No. Stability still depends on the equations, method and step size.

quiz.question: What is a useful check beyond watching the animation?
quiz.answer: Compare to an analytic solution or conserved quantity and perform timestep-refinement tests.

modules.title: Probability, statistics and evidence
modules.project: Create a reproducible benchmark experiment and a loot-distribution simulation. Report assumptions, uncertainty, representative workloads and one result that did not support the original hypothesis.

lessons.title: Probability and conditional reasoning
lessons.outcome: Model uncertainty without confusing independent and conditional events.
lessons.teach:
Probability assigns weights to events under a model. Conditional probability restricts attention to cases where another event occurred. Independence means learning one event does not change the probability of the other; it is an assumption to justify, not a default for every repeated observation.
Bayes' rule reverses conditioning using prior probabilities and evidence likelihoods. Rare-event base rates matter when interpreting an apparently accurate detector. In games, these ideas apply to randomized systems, telemetry and testing. A measured frequency approaches a model probability only under suitable sampling assumptions; a small sample can be very noisy.
lessons.example: For independent fair coin flips, the probability of two heads is 1/4. If the second outcome is deliberately copied from the first, the probability is 1/2, demonstrating why dependence changes the calculation.
lessons.lab: Simulate independent and dependent binary events. Build a small contingency table for a hypothetical bug detector. Pass: calculate both P(alert|bug) and P(bug|alert) and explain why they differ.
lessons.reading: R09: probability, conditional probability and Bayes' theorem.

quiz.question: What is the probability of two independent events with probabilities 0.5 and 0.2 both occurring?
quiz.answer: 0.1, the product under the stated independence assumption.

quiz.question: Is P(A|B) generally equal to P(B|A)?
quiz.answer: No. They condition on different populations.

quiz.question: Why do rare-event base rates matter for an alert?
quiz.answer: Even a small false-positive rate can produce many alerts when true events are very rare.

lessons.title: Random variables, distributions and sampling
lessons.outcome: Distinguish an expected value from a guaranteed outcome.
lessons.teach:
A random variable maps outcomes to numbers. Its expectation is a probability-weighted average; variance measures spread around that average. A distribution describes the possible values and their probabilities. Bernoulli, binomial and normal models have different assumptions and should not be chosen only because their names are familiar.
Pseudorandom generators are deterministic algorithms with internal state. A seed supports repeatable experiments, but a generator suitable for gameplay is not automatically suitable for security. Sampling can be biased by how data is collected. Use separate random streams when independent subsystems should not change each other's results merely by making extra draws.
lessons.example: A reward of 10 with probability 0.2 and 0 otherwise has expected value 2. A player still receives either 10 or 0 on one trial, not necessarily 2.
lessons.lab: Implement a weighted reward sampler and compare observed frequencies to the intended distribution over several sample sizes. Pass: record seed, generator, counts and expected values; explain finite-sample variation.
lessons.reading: R09: random variables, expectation and variance; R04: random reference.

quiz.question: What is the expectation of 20 with probability 0.25 and 0 otherwise?
Does an expectation of 5 guarantee a reward of 5 on a trial?
quiz.answer: No. It describes an average under the model, not an individual outcome.

quiz.question: Why separate random streams for unrelated systems?
quiz.answer: An extra draw in one system should not unintentionally alter another system's sequence.

lessons.title: Inference, uncertainty and benchmark design
lessons.outcome: Compare implementations without hiding variance or bias.
lessons.teach:
A sample statistic estimates a property of a larger process. Confidence intervals express uncertainty under a sampling model; they are not a probability that a fixed frequentist parameter lies in a specific realized interval. Hypothesis tests require defined assumptions and do not measure practical importance by themselves.
For performance work, control workload, build mode, warmup and environmental changes. Use repeated independent runs where possible; adjacent frames are often correlated. Report distributions and tail latency rather than only an average. A statistically detectable difference may be too small to matter, while a rare long pause can be important despite little change in the mean.
lessons.example: Implementation A might average 5 ms but occasionally take 100 ms; B might average 6 ms with no large pauses in the tested sample. The preferred design depends on throughput and latency requirements, not the mean alone.
lessons.lab: Compare two implementations using the same inputs, randomized test order and repeated runs. Pass: report median, a tail percentile, sample count and limitations; distinguish observations from causal claims.
lessons.reading: R09: confidence intervals, hypothesis testing and experimental reasoning.

quiz.question: Why can adjacent frame times violate an independence assumption?
quiz.answer: They share workload phases, caches, thermal state and other correlated conditions.

quiz.question: Does a small p-value establish a large useful improvement?
quiz.answer: No. Statistical evidence and practical effect size are different questions.

quiz.question: Why report a tail percentile alongside a mean?
quiz.answer: It exposes slow cases that can affect responsiveness despite an acceptable average.

lessons.title: Regression, correlation and ethical telemetry
lessons.outcome: Fit a model while recognizing confounding and data limits.
lessons.teach:
Regression relates an outcome to predictors under a chosen model. Correlation is association, not proof of causation. A confounder can influence both the apparent cause and the outcome. Models should be evaluated on held-out observations or a suitable validation scheme, not only on the data used to fit them.
Telemetry collection should have a defined purpose and minimize unnecessary personal data. For course projects, use synthetic or consented data rather than harvesting real players. Do not optimize only the easiest-to-measure metric. Session length, for example, is not equivalent to enjoyment, accessibility or wellbeing.
lessons.example: Players with better hardware may both buy more games and achieve higher frame rates. Observing a purchase/frame-rate correlation does not establish that purchases caused faster rendering.
lessons.lab: Fit a simple performance model using entity count and measured update time. Hold out some workloads. Pass: report prediction error and one confounder; write a short data-minimization plan for the experiment.
lessons.reading: R09: regression and inference; R01: ethics and data-management breadth.

quiz.question: Why is training-set fit alone insufficient?
quiz.answer: A model can overfit and fail on new observations or workloads.

quiz.question: What is a confounder?
quiz.answer: A variable that influences both the proposed explanatory factor and the outcome, complicating causal interpretation.

quiz.question: Why should telemetry collect only what the question requires?
quiz.answer: It reduces privacy exposure and unnecessary data handling while keeping the experiment focused.

modules.title: Signals, optimization and numerical foundations
modules.project: Complete Gate B: a mathematical engineering notebook plus tested transforms, numerical integration, signal filtering and an uncertainty-aware experiment.

lessons.title: Multivariable calculus and gradients
lessons.outcome: Use partial derivatives to reason about spatial fields and optimization.
lessons.teach:
A multivariable function depends on several inputs. A partial derivative varies one input while holding the others fixed. The gradient collects partial derivatives and points toward steepest local increase under the usual Euclidean metric. The Jacobian describes the local linear behavior of a vector-valued function.
Gradients support terrain normals, inverse kinematics and parameter fitting. A gradient is local information, not a guarantee of the global best direction over a large step. Chain-rule reasoning must follow every transformation. Numerical derivatives are useful checks for analytic code, but choose perturbations that account for scale and rounding.
lessons.example: For f(x,y)=x*x+y*y, the gradient is (2*x,2*y). At (3,4), it is (6,8). Taking a small step in the negative gradient direction reduces f locally.
lessons.lab: Derive gradients for three functions and check them with centered differences. Pass: test nonzero and stationary points, vary perturbation size and report errors rather than claiming exact equality.
lessons.reading: R07: linearization foundations; R23: geometric differential quantities; use the program's multivariable extension reading.

quiz.question: What is the gradient of x*x + 3*y*y?
What does a Jacobian describe?
quiz.answer: The first-order local mapping from small input changes to output changes for a vector-valued function.

quiz.question: Does a zero gradient always identify a minimum?
quiz.answer: No. It may identify a maximum, saddle or other stationary point.

lessons.title: Sampling, aliasing and Fourier ideas
lessons.outcome: Explain why discrete samples can misrepresent a continuous signal.
lessons.teach:
Sampling records a signal at discrete positions or times. Different high-frequency signals can produce the same samples, creating aliasing. Reconstruction needs assumptions about bandwidth and a suitable filter. For a strictly band-limited signal, the familiar sampling criterion requires a rate greater than twice its highest frequency; practical systems need transition bands and margin.
The Fourier viewpoint decomposes signals into frequency components. It connects audio, textures, animation and display artifacts. Increasing resolution helps only relative to the signal content. Filtering before downsampling removes frequencies that the lower rate cannot represent; filtering afterward cannot generally recover information already aliased.
lessons.example: A 900 Hz tone sampled at 1000 samples/second can appear as a 100 Hz tone. The samples do not uniquely preserve the original high-frequency oscillation.
lessons.lab: Generate low- and high-frequency sine samples, then downsample a checker pattern with and without prefiltering. Pass: explain the artifacts using frequency content rather than calling them random noise.
lessons.reading: R10: sampling and Fourier representation; R23: Sampling and Reconstruction.

quiz.question: What is the Nyquist frequency at 48,000 samples/second?
quiz.answer: 24,000 Hz, the half-sampling-rate boundary; practical filtering requires additional care.

quiz.question: Why filter before downsampling?
quiz.answer: To remove frequencies that would fold into misleading lower frequencies at the new sample rate.

quiz.question: Can post-filtering always undo aliasing?
quiz.answer: No. Distinct original signals may already have become indistinguishable in the samples.

lessons.title: Convolution, filters and systems
lessons.outcome: Predict a filter's effect on data and latency.
lessons.teach:
Convolution combines a signal with a kernel by weighted summation of shifted values. A moving average smooths high-frequency variation, but it also changes edges and can introduce delay depending on implementation. A linear time-invariant system is characterized by its impulse response under the model assumptions.
Boundary handling is part of a filter definition. Zero padding, wrapping and edge replication produce different results. Filters also have numeric and performance costs. In audio, a stable and bounded processing path is essential; in images, color-space assumptions matter when averaging values. Test an impulse and a constant signal before trusting a complex input.
lessons.example: A three-sample average of [3,6,9] is 6. Sliding this kernel across a sequence produces a smoothed sequence; values near either end require an explicit boundary policy.
lessons.lab: Implement a one-dimensional convolution with documented boundary handling. Test an impulse, a constant and a step. Pass: predict the output before running and identify the filter's delay convention.
lessons.reading: R10: convolution, impulse response and linear time-invariant systems.

quiz.question: What does convolving with an impulse reveal?
quiz.answer: The filter's impulse response, including its alignment convention.

quiz.question: What is the average of 2, 5 and 8?
Why is boundary handling not an implementation footnote?
quiz.answer: It changes the mathematical result at the edges and may create visible or audible artifacts.

lessons.title: Optimization, conditioning and approximation budgets
lessons.outcome: Choose an objective and distinguish convergence from correctness.
lessons.teach:
Optimization minimizes or maximizes a specified objective under constraints. Gradient descent takes steps opposite the gradient; its behavior depends on step size, scaling and the shape of the objective. A local optimum need not be global. Constraints can be as important as the objective, such as keeping error below a visible threshold while reducing work.
Numerical engineering combines error sources: model approximations, finite precision, sampling and iterative termination. Define an error budget and a reference case. More iterations can reduce one error while leaving others unchanged. Stop according to a justified criterion and report failure to converge rather than silently returning a plausible number.
lessons.example: For f(x)=(x-3)^2, gradient descent uses x_next=x-alpha*2*(x-3). An excessively large alpha can oscillate or diverge even though the function has a simple minimum.
lessons.lab: Implement gradient descent on a quadratic and a two-variable problem. Pass: compare step sizes, record residuals and state a stopping rule; complete Gate B with no unsupported claim of global optimality.
lessons.reading: R07: least squares and conditioning; R23: numerical utilities; graduate optimization reading in the handbook.

quiz.question: Where is the minimum of (x-3)^2?
quiz.answer: At x=3, with objective value zero.

quiz.question: Why can reducing step size help an unstable iteration?
quiz.answer: It can prevent updates from overshooting the region where local information is useful, though convergence can become slower.

quiz.question: What should happen when an iterative method reaches its iteration limit?
quiz.answer: Report nonconvergence or the achieved residual explicitly rather than pretending the requested accuracy was met.
